claim: Yersinia pestis is among the most virulent pathogens known to cause disease in humans.
source: The bacterium Yersinia pestis is among the most virulent pathogens known to cause disease in humans.
evidence: This is a general statement about Y. pestis virulence that draws from established scientific knowledge about this pathogen.

claim: Yersinia pestis is an existing threat to public health as the cause of both emerging and re-emerging rodent-derived epidemics in many regions of the world.
source: As the agent of plague it is an existing threat to public health as the cause of both emerging and re-emerging rodent-derived epidemics in many regions of the world (Duplantier et al., 2005; Vogler et al., 2011; Gage and Kosoy, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Duplantier et al., 2005; Vogler et al., 2011; Gage and Kosoy, 2005).

claim: Yersinia pestis was involved in three major historical pandemics.
source: This, and its confirmed involvement in three major historical pandemics, have made it the subject of intense study.
evidence: This claim is supported by established historical and scientific knowledge about plague pandemics.

claim: The first pandemic, also known as the Justinian Plague, occurred from the 6th through the 8th centuries.
source: The first pandemic, also known as the Justinian Plague, occurred from the 6th through the 8th centuries
evidence: This is a historical fact about the timing of the first plague pandemic.

claim: The second pandemic spanned the 14th to the 18th centuries.
source: the second pandemic spanned the 14th to the 18th centuries
evidence: This is a historical fact about the timing of the second plague pandemic.

claim: The third pandemic started in the 19th century and persists to the present day.
source: the third pandemic started in the 19th century and persists to the present day.
evidence: This is a historical and contemporary fact about the third plague pandemic.

claim: Attempts to date the evolutionary history of Y. pestis using molecular clocks have been compromised by extensive variation in nucleotide substitution rates among lineages.
source: Attempts to date the evolutionary history of Y. pestis using molecular clocks have been compromised by extensive variation in nucleotide substitution rates among lineages (Cui et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies (Cui et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2014) that documented variation in substitution rates.

claim: There is considerable uncertainty over how long Y. pestis has caused epidemic disease in human populations.
source: such that there is considerable uncertainty over how long this pathogen has caused epidemic disease in human populations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the preceding statement about compromised molecular clock dating due to rate variation.

claim: There has been debate as to whether Y. pestis was the principal cause of the three historical pandemics.
source: In addition, there has been lively debate as to whether or not it was the principal cause of the three historical pandemics (Cohn, 2008; Scott and Duncan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies (Cohn, 2008; Scott and Duncan, 2005) that debated Y. pestis as the cause.

claim: Extant lineages of Y. pestis circulated during the third pandemic.
source: It is well established that extant lineages of Y. pestis circulated during the third pandemic (Achtman et al., 2004; Morelli et al., 2010)

claim: Ancient DNA studies have unequivocally demonstrated Y. pestis involvement in the early phase of the first pandemic in the 6th century.
source: various ancient DNA studies have now unequivocally demonstrated its involvement in the early phase of the first pandemic in the 6th century (Harbeck et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two ancient DNA studies (Harbeck et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2014).

claim: Ancient DNA studies have unequivocally demonstrated Y. pestis involvement in the Black Death (1347–1351), which marks the beginning of the second plague pandemic.
source: various ancient DNA studies have now unequivocally demonstrated its involvement in the early phase of the first pandemic in the 6th century (Harbeck et al., 2013; Wagner et al., 2014) and the Black Death (1347–1351), which marks the beginning of the second plague pandemic (Bos et al., 2011; Haensch et al., 2010; Schuenemann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three ancient DNA studies (Bos et al., 2011; Haensch et al., 2010; Schuenemann et al., 2011).

claim: All three pandemics likely arose from natural rodent foci in Asia and spread along trade routes to Europe and other parts of the world.
source: All three pandemics likely arose from natural rodent foci in Asia and spread along trade routes to Europe and other parts of the world (Morelli et al., 2010; Wagner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies (Morelli et al., 2010; Wagner et al., 2014) and involves inference about pandemic origins.

claim: The strains associated with the first and second pandemics represent independent emergence events from rodent reservoirs in Asia.
source: The strains associated with the first and second pandemics represent independent emergence events from these rodent reservoirs in Asia.

claim: The on-going third pandemic originated in Asia.
source: The on-going third pandemic also originated in Asia

claim: During the second pandemic there were hundreds and perhaps thousands of local plague outbreaks in human populations throughout Europe.
